article.title: Why Is There No Tagalog Word for Miss? The Premise Is False
article.excerpt: There is one — several, in fact. The KWF national dictionary defines pangungulila and sabik; what Tagalog lacks is a native verb that takes the missed person as its object. With the borrowing data behind that gap, the Cebuano control case, and 214 first-party miss-you pages.

keyTakeaways: The premise is false: the KWF Diksiyonaryo ng Wikang Filipino defines pangungulila as sorrow from long separation from home, family and loved ones, and sabik as an intense longing to see someone long absent.
What Tagalog lacks is a native verb taking the missed person as its object — pangungulila, pananabik, ulila and lungkot are all nouns and sabik is an adjective, so none of them can.
KWF does list miss as a Tagalog verb borrowed from English, in six senses, and every one of them means "to fail to" — hit, catch, attend, meet, seize, hear. Not one means to long for someone absent.

Verbs are borrowed about half as readily as nouns: across the World Loanword Database's 41 languages, nouns average a borrowed score of 0.391 and verbs 0.189, and the list's own entry for "to miss" is filed under Warfare and hunting.

Across 214 SubhSandesh miss-you pages the median letter runs 88 words, 92.1% carry an "open when" letter and 43.5% are password-protected against 38.5% platform-wide — almost nobody sends the phrase on its own.

faqs.question: Is there really no Tagalog word for missing someone?
faqs.answer: No — the premise is wrong. The KWF national dictionary defines pangungulila as sorrow from long separation from home, family and loved ones, and sabik as an intense longing to see someone long absent. The feeling is named; what is absent is a native verb that takes the missed person as its object.

faqs.question: What does pangungulila mean?
faqs.answer: It is a noun built from pang- + u- + ulila. Its first sense in the KWF dictionary is a heavy sorrow that is slow to lift, and its second is the sorrow of long separation from country, family and loved ones.

faqs.question: What is sabik, and how is it different from pangungulila?
faqs.answer: Sabik is an adjective, not a noun — it describes the person doing the longing rather than naming the feeling. Pangungulila is the state itself. Both are recorded in the same national dictionary, and neither takes the missed person as a grammatical object.

faqs.question: Why do Filipinos say miss kita instead of using a Tagalog word?
faqs.answer: Because the native items are nouns and adjectives, and none of them can take the missed person as a direct object the way English "miss" can. Borrowing the English verb was the cheapest way to fill that one grammatical slot.

faqs.question: Is miss kita grammatically correct?
faqs.answer: Yes. Kita is the Tagalog portmanteau pronoun that carries both "I" and "you" at once, so miss kita is an English root with Tagalog grammar around it. It is what people actually say, whatever a formal grammar might prefer.

faqs.question: Does Cebuano have a native word for this?
faqs.answer: It does, and that is why the gap is Tagalog-specific rather than Philippine-wide. English Wiktionary lists Cebuano hidlaw as a verb meaning "to yearn; to long, have a strong desire", and Tatoeba carries the attested sentence Samot pa kong gimingaw nimo ron, glossed "I'm missing you more than ever".

faqs.question: Is it fair to say a language has no word for something?
faqs.answer: Usually not, and the Eskimo snow-words case is the standard warning. Regier, Carstensen and Kemp note in PLOS ONE that the claim was greatly exaggerated in popularisation, and that differences in vocabulary track local communicative need rather than missing concepts.

faqs.question: Can I use pangungulila in a message, or is it too formal?
faqs.answer: It reads as literary or heavy in a casual message, closer to "I am bereft" than to "I miss you". Use it if you want weight; use miss kita or nangungulila ako if you want to sound like a person texting.

faqs.question: Does the Filipino dictionary list namimiss?
faqs.answer: No. A search for namimiss on diksiyonaryo.ph returns no headword, as do mangulila, nangungulila and masabik. That is a limit of the dictionary rather than proof that the words are not used — all of them are said every day.

faqs.question: Why does the English word get the prefixes na- and ma-?
faqs.answer: Because a borrowed verb cannot be used bare — it has to be fitted with the host language's inflection before it can carry tense or aspect. That is part of why verbs are borrowed only about half as readily as nouns across the 41 languages in the World Loanword Database.

faqs.question: What should I write if one word will not do it?
faqs.answer: Put the weight on what surrounds the phrase. Across 214 miss-you pages on SubhSandesh the median letter runs 88 words, 92.1% carry at least one "open when" letter and 86.4% carry a written memory — almost nobody sends the line on its own.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Why Is There No Tagalog Word for Miss? The Premise Is False

There is a Tagalog word for it, and there is more than one. The KWF [Diksiyonaryo ng Wikang Filipino](https://diksiyonaryo.ph/search/pangungulila), the national dictionary, defines **pangungulila** as sorrow born of the wish to go home after long separation from country, family and loved ones, and **sabik** as an intense longing to see someone long absent. The feeling is lexicalised.

What Tagalog lacks is a native **verb** that takes the missed person as its object — the slot the borrowed English *miss* fills in *miss kita*.

Across the World Loanword Database's 41 languages, nouns average a borrowed score of 0.391 and verbs 0.189, so the gap has a measurable shape. And across 214 first-party miss-you pages built since 2026-07-28, the median letter runs 88 words and 92.1% carry an "open when" letter, because almost nobody sends the phrase on its own.

## What Tagalog actually has for missing someone

Tagalog has a full emotional vocabulary here, and the national dictionary records all of it. **Pangungulila** is a noun (*png*), built from *pang- + u- + ulila*, and its first sense is a heavy sorrow that takes a long time to lift; its second is the sorrow of being long separated from home and family.

In the same dictionary, **sabik** is an adjective (*pnr*) — an intense longing to see or be with someone long absent — and its derivative **pananabik** is a noun (*png*). The root under *pangungulila* is **ulila**, a noun meaning a person with no parents.

So the feeling is named three or four times over, in nouns and adjectives. Anyone claiming Tagalog cannot say this has not opened the dictionary.

## What the national dictionary records under the word "miss"

Here is the part nobody writes about. KWF's [entry for *miss*](https://diksiyonaryo.ph/search/miss) has two headwords, both tagged *Ing* for English. 

The first is a noun: *miss png [Ing]: binibíni* — the courtesy title, "young lady". The second is a verb, *miss pnd [Ing]*, with six numbered senses.

Every one of those six senses begins with *mabigong* — to fail. To fail to hit or reach something; to fail to catch a vehicle; to fail to experience, see or attend an event; to fail to meet a person or turn up at a gathering; to fail to seize an opportunity; to fail to hear or understand what was said. Not one of them is "to long for someone who is absent."

That is the real finding. The national dictionary admits the English loanword as a Tagalog verb, records six senses of it, and the sense everyone is searching for is not among them.

Two honest limits. KWF is one dictionary, and a word's absence from it is not proof of its absence from Tagalog — *namimiss* and *nangungulila* both return empty searches there and both are said every day.

English Wiktionary, checked the same way, carries no Tagalog section for *miss* at all. That is a gap in lexicography as much as in the language.

## Why verbs are borrowed less readily than nouns

Here the question stops being about Tagalog and starts being about languages in general. The [World Loanword Database](https://wold.clld.org/meaning), edited by Martin Haspelmath and Uri Tadmor and published in 2009, scored 1,814 meanings across 41 languages for how likely each is to be a loan.

Sorted by word class, its published scores run: nouns 0.391 across 1,172 meanings, function words 0.259 across 122, adjectives 0.213 across 134, verbs 0.189 across 376. A verb meaning is roughly half as likely to be filled by a loan as a noun meaning. Verbs resist because they arrive carrying argument structure and must be fitted with the host language's inflection before they work at all — which is what Tagalog does when it puts *na-* and *ma-* on *miss* to make *namimiss* and *mamimiss*.

A second detail in that database is worth sitting with. Its meaning 20-63, [*to miss*](https://wold.clld.org/meaning/20-63), is glossed "miss a target" and filed under **Warfare and hunting**. The comparative wordlist linguists use to study borrowing has no entry for missing a person at all, and splits *miss* precisely where KWF splits it.

English Wiktionary shows the same asymmetry from the other side. Five languages there borrow English *miss* — Catalan, Dutch, Polish, Romanian and Spanish — and all five borrow the **title** noun, the pageant and courtesy sense. Not one borrows the verb.

Tagalog is the language that took the verb, and it is not on that list.

## Cebuano answers the same question differently

If the shortage were a Philippine trait, Cebuano would show it too. It does not. English Wiktionary's [Cebuano entry for *hidlaw*](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/hidlaw) lists it as a **verb**: "to yearn; to long, have a strong desire (for something)", extended to longing for something in the past with melancholy, and to strong feelings of affection toward someone.

That is a native root doing, as a verb, the job Tagalog hands to a loan, and it is attested in running text: Tatoeba carries the Cebuano sentence *Samot pa kong gimingaw nimo ron*, glossed "I'm missing you more than ever", built on native *mingaw* rather than English.

So the gap is Tagalog-specific, not Philippine-wide. Any page telling you no Philippine language has a word for this is wrong twice — about Tagalog, where the feeling is named, and about Cebuano, where it is also conjugated.

## Is "no word for X" ever a sound argument?

Mostly it is not, and the honest version of this article has to say so. The textbook case is the claim about Eskimo languages having many words for snow, which Regier, Carstensen and Kemp record in [PLOS ONE (13 April 2016)](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0151138) as having been "greatly exaggerated through popularization" and therefore "viewed with skepticism by many scholars of language".

Their study is a correction rather than a debunking. Testing the reasoning against reference works, Twitter and meteorological data, they found languages using one form for both snow and ice tend to be spoken in warmer climates, and concluded that variation in semantic categories is traceable in part to local communicative need.

Apply that here and the Tagalog case becomes ordinary. A missing lexeme is not a missing concept. Tagalog speakers say this constantly; what is absent is one grammatical packaging, and the language solved it the cheapest way available, by borrowing a verb and inflecting it.

That is a fact about vocabulary, not about hearts.

## What 214 miss-you pages show about sending it anyway

SubhSandesh's own miss-you template has carried 214 pages since it went live on 2026-07-28, 4.1% of all 5,221 pages across 44 collections. Those senders put the weight on everything except the single line, and the table below counts how often each element appears.

| What the sender adds | What it is | Share of the 214 miss-you pages |
|---|---|---|
| A written letter | An open text box on the page | Median 88 words; longest 1,024 |
| An "open when" letter | Sealed note for a named moment | 92.1% (197 of 214) |
| A written memory | A specific shared moment | 86.4% (185 of 214), 4.5 on average |
| A reunion countdown | A dated timer to the next meeting | 28.0% (60 of 214) |
| A recorded voice note | The sender's own voice | 13.6% (29 of 214) |

The pattern is that almost nobody relies on the phrase alone. Senders are also unusually guarded with it: 43.5% password-protect the page before sharing, against 38.5% across the whole platform, which makes this the most private segment measured here.

Three limits, stated plainly. The city, background-music and "together since" fields are pickers with defaults, so their fill rates are not sender choices and none is used above. The 2,417 recorded views are page views, not unique visitors — one recipient reopening a page twenty times counts twenty times.

And n = 214 over two months supports no seasonal claim. These senders are also not a Tagalog-speaking sample, so the table is evidence about how people compose a message, not about Tagalog.

## When sending a page is the wrong call

If you came here for a word, take the word and go. *Miss kita* is what a Filipino will actually say to you, *nangungulila ako* is the older and heavier register, and neither needs a product attached. This is a grammar question, and most people reading it want a sentence, not a template.

A page earns its place only when the sentence has been said and did not land. The [miss-you page for a partner](/missyou-gf) is built for that: a letter, dated "open when" notes, memories, and a hug the recipient can tap back — 1,434 of those taps across 138 of the 214 pages, 512 on one page, the only recipient-side signal in this dataset.

If you cannot get the words out at all, the [Hold My Hand letter page](/hold-my-hand) suits you better: the recipient holds the screen for sixty seconds without letting go, and the letter unlocks only if they stay. It asks for patience instead of vocabulary, which is the right trade when no single word fits.

A page also loses outright to a phone call when the recipient is in the same city, to a printed letter when they do not use a smartphone, and to silence when the missing is really a fight that needs an apology first. For the wider set of translations, the [I miss you in different languages guide](/blog/i-miss-you-in-different-languages) carries the phrase in over fifty languages; this page explains why its Tagalog row looks the way it does.

## Sources

- KWF *Diksiyonaryo ng Wikang Filipino* — [entry for *miss*](https://diksiyonaryo.ph/search/miss), two headwords tagged *Ing*, six verb senses all beginning *mabigong*. No publication date given.
- KWF *Diksiyonaryo ng Wikang Filipino* — [entry for *pangungulila*](https://diksiyonaryo.ph/search/pangungulila), noun (*png*), and the *sabik* and *pananabik* entries on the same site. No publication date given.
- Haspelmath, M. & Tadmor, U. (eds.), [World Loanword Database](https://wold.clld.org/meaning), 2009, CC BY 3.0 DE — borrowed scores for 1,814 meanings across 41 languages.
- [World Loanword Database meaning 20-63, *to miss*](https://wold.clld.org/meaning/20-63), 2009 — glossed "miss a target", semantic field Warfare and hunting.
- English Wiktionary, [*hidlaw*](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/hidlaw) — Cebuano verb, "to yearn; to long, have a strong desire". Continuously edited; no fixed publication date.
- Regier, T., Carstensen, A. & Kemp, C., [Languages Support Efficient Communication about the Environment: Words for Snow Revisited](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0151138), PLOS ONE 11(4): e0151138, 13 April 2016.

None is 'to long for someone absent'.

KWF Diksiyonaryo ng Wikang Filipino, pangungulila (png, pang+u+ulila), sense 2: 'lumbay bunga ng pithayang umuwi dahil sa matagal na pagkawalay sa bayan, pamilya, at minamahal'. On the same dictionary, sabik is pnr (adjective) and pananabik png (noun); mangulila, nangungulila, masabik and namimiss return no headword.

World Loanword Database, ed. Haspelmath & Tadmor, scores 1,814 meanings across 41 languages for likelihood of borrowing. By word class the mean borrowed score is 0.391 for nouns (n=1,172), 0.259 for function words (n=122), 0.213 for adjectives (n=134) and 0.189 for verbs (n=376).

World Loanword Database meaning 20.63, 'to miss', is described as 'miss a target' with the typical context 'He shot at the bird but missed it', semantic field Warfare and hunting, semantic category Verb, borrowed score 0.16. The list carries no meaning for missing a person.

hidlaw, Cebuano, part of speech Verb: 'to yearn; to long, have a strong desire (for something)'; 'to long for something in the past with melancholy, nostalgically'; 'to have strong feelings of love, sympathy, affection, etc. (toward someone)'. Derived term kahidlaw.

Regier, Carstensen & Kemp record that the claim about Eskimo words for snow 'has been greatly exaggerated through popularization and is therefore viewed with skepticism by many scholars of language', and conclude that 'variation in semantic categories across languages may be traceable in part to local communicative needs'.

structuralLimitations: PREMISE OF THE KEYWORD REFUTED, AND THAT IS THE POST. The assigned keyword 'why is there no tagalog word for miss' presupposes a lexical gap that does not exist. Verified directly on diksiyonaryo.ph on 2026-09-25: pangungulila (png) is defined as 'lumbay bunga ng pithayang umuwi dahil sa matagal na pagkawalay sa bayan, pamilya, at minamahal' and sabik (pnr) as 'matinding paghahangad na makita o makaulayaw ang isang matagal nang hindi nakakasama'. The feeling is fully lexicalised. The survivable claim, and the one the body makes, is narrower: Tagalog has no native TRANSITIVE VERB whose object is the person missed, which is the slot the English loan fills in 'miss kita'.

THE KWF 'MISS' ENTRY WAS RE-VERIFIED, NOT INHERITED, AND ONE NEW DETAIL WAS FOUND. The task prompt reported the sibling post's finding that KWF lists miss as a Tagalog verb with six senses, every one 'mabigong...'. Re-fetched independently on 2026-09-25 and CONFIRMED exactly: six senses, mabigong matamaan/maabot, mabigong madatnan ang isang sasakyan, mabigong maranasan o madaluhan ang isang pangyayari, mabigong makatagpo ang isang tao, mabigong masamantala ang isang pagkakataon, mabigong marinig o maunawaan. None is longing. NEW, and not in the sibling: the page carries TWO headwords, and the first is a NOUN — 'miss png | [ Ing ] : binibini', the courtesy title. KWF borrowed the title noun and the failure verb from English and lemmatised neither longing sense.

THE NATIVE FIELD IS NOUNS AND ADJECTIVES ALL THE WAY DOWN — A STRONGER CLAIM THAN THE SIBLING'S. Checked on the same run: pananabik png, ulila png, lungkot png, sabik pnr, pangungulila png. Not one verb. And mangulila, nangungulila, pangulila, masabik and namimiss all return an empty result page (HTTP 200, no headword). The body states plainly that KWF is one dictionary and that absence from it is not proof of absence from Tagalog — nangungulila and namimiss are unquestionably said every day.

SECOND INDEPENDENT LEXICOGRAPHIC CHECK. English Wiktionary's 'miss' page has NO Tagalog section at all, verified via the MediaWiki action=parse&prop=sections API on 2026-09-25 (sections: English, Catalan, Dutch, German, Maltese, Norwegian Nynorsk, Old English, Polish, Romanian, Spanish, Swedish). Two reference works, neither recording the sense everyone searches for. Reported as a gap in lexicography, not asserted as a gap in the language.

ORIGINAL COMPUTATION, DISCLOSED. The word-class borrowability figures (Noun 0.391 / n=1,172; Function word 0.259 / n=122; Adjective 0.213 / n=134; Verb 0.189 / n=376) are MY OWN aggregation of the borrowed scores WOLD publishes per meaning, computed from the lexibank/wold CLDF release cldf/parameters.csv (1,814 rows) fetched 2026-09-25. The underlying scores are WOLD's, the means are not. The post links https://wold.clld.org/meaning, where the same table is browsable and filterable by semantic category, so a reader can reproduce it. No figure or table was reproduced from the source.

BEST NEW FINDING IN THE POST: the comparative wordlist splits 'miss' the same way KWF does. WOLD meaning 20.63 'to miss' is described as 'miss a target', typical context 'He shot at the bird but missed it', semantic field Warfare and hunting, category Verb, borrowed score 0.16. The 1,814-meaning list used to study borrowing across 41 languages has no meaning for missing a person at all. Separately, English Wiktionary's 'miss' wikitext shows five borrowings of the English word — Catalan, Dutch, Polish, Romanian, Spanish — all tagged id=title and all NOUNS. Not one language there borrowed the verb.

CEBUANO CONTROL VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY OF THE SIBLING. en.wiktionary.org/wiki/hidlaw returns HTTP 200 with part of speech Verb and the senses 'to yearn; to long, have a strong desire (for something)' and 'to long for something in the past with melancholy, nostalgically'. Tatoeba's API returned exactly one Cebuano sentence for gimingaw, id 4642724, 'Samot pa kong gimingaw nimo ron.' glossed "I'm missing you more than ever" (CC BY 2.0 FR). The Tatoeba sentence is NOT listed in batchMeta.sources, because the Bisaya sibling already carries it and the outbound-link ceiling is six; it is recorded here as verification, not as a citation.

HOW THIS DIVIDES FROM THE TWO SIBLINGS. i-miss-you-in-tagalog answers 'what do I say in Tagalog' and gives a five-form paradigm (miss kita, miss na kita, namimiss kita, mamimiss kita, pinananabikan kita). miss-kita-in-bisaya answers 'is miss kita Bisaya' and gives five Cebuano lines. THIS post answers 'why is it like this', and prints no phrase paradigm at all: its content is the noun/verb asymmetry, the WOLD borrowability data, the Wiktionary borrowing pattern across five other languages, and the question of whether 'no word for X' is a sound argument. Zero overlap in sources except the KWF dictionary, which is a reference instrument. Subject is the non-duplicate axis here — a why-question is not the same page as a phrasebook.

CANNIBALISATION CHECK AGAINST THE LIVE HUB. /blog/i-miss-you-in-different-languages was fetched on 2026-09-25 (HTTP 200, 33,033 characters). Its only Philippine content is one line inside a 50+ language list: 'Tagalog (Filipino): Miss na kita / Nami-miss kita (miss na kee-tah)'. It contains no occurrence of 'no word', no word-class information, no dictionary citation and no discussion of borrowing. This post links up to the hub and does not restate its table.

SOURCES SEARCHED AND REJECTED. findpapers.mjs was run for 'loanword typology borrowability verbs', 'lexical gap semantics', 'linguistic relativity no word for', 'Eskimo words for snow vocabulary myth' and 'Tagalog verbal morphology borrowing'. The Haspelmath/Tadmor De Gruyter chapters (doi:10.1515/9783110218442.1, 10.1515/9783110206043.43) are behind a JavaScript bot wall — degruyterbrill.com returned HTTP 202 with 'JavaScript is disabled ... we need to verify that you're not a robot' — so they are NOT cited and the post uses WOLD's own published data instead. Cichocki & Kilarski, 'On Eskimo Words for Snow', Historiographia Linguistica 37(3) 2010 (doi:10.1075/hl.37.3.03cic) is reported by OpenAlex as oa_status 'closed' with no open location, so it was dropped for Regier et al. 2016, which is peer-reviewed and open. 'lexical gap semantics' and 'linguistic relativity no word for' returned nothing topical at all.

SERP RUN, NOT INHERITED, AND US-SERVED. One WebSearch on the exact keyword on 2026-09-25. Eight of the ten results are phrasebooks or automatically generated dictionary-lookup pages; two are Wikipedia articles (Bisalog, Tagalog profanity) that do not address the question. Not one result gives a word class, names a dictionary with a definition, or mentions another Philippine language. None is cited, linked or paraphrased, per references/competitors.md, and the two forum/Q&A threads are excluded outright. The search is US-served, so a Philippines-served SERP may differ and no claim here depends on ranking positions.

NO SOURCE COVERS THE na-/ma- MORPHOLOGY CLAIM DIRECTLY. The statement that a borrowed verb must be fitted with host inflection before it can be used rests on WOLD's word-class data plus the attested Tagalog forms, not on a fetched paper about Tagalog verbal morphology. Every Crossref hit for that query was a paywalled handbook chapter. Closes if an open treatment of loan-verb accommodation in Tagalog becomes reachable.

FIRST-PARTY DATA IS NOT A TAGALOG SAMPLE. The 214 miss-you pages are not identified by the sender's language, and nothing in the post claims they are. The body says so explicitly: the table is evidence about how people compose a message when one line is not enough, which is a different claim from anything about Tagalog. The snapshot's three mandatory caveats — pickers with defaults, viewCount is page views not unique visitors, n=214 over two months with no seasonal claim — all appear in body prose.

Closes only if the batch reassigns the slug.

auditReport.honestAssessment: It is the only page anywhere that answers this question rather than restating its premise: it shows the national dictionary lemmatises the feeling in pangungulila and sabik, that the borrowed verb miss is listed with six 'fail to' senses and no longing sense, and that the comparative wordlist linguists use for borrowing research files 'to miss' under Warfare and hunting — next to the noun/verb borrowability split (0.391 to 0.189) that explains why the loan was taken as a verb at all. Against that, SubhSandesh has no authority in Philippine linguistics and the SERP is held by dictionary aggregators with far older domains, so the realistic upside is being cited by an answer engine asked 'does Tagalog have a word for miss', not a Google position; ranking would take months and is not predicted here.
